{
  "text": "## The Efficacy of Postoperative Prophylactic Antibiotics in Orthognathic Surgery: A Prospective Study in Le Fort I Osteotomy and Bilateral Intraoral Vertical Ramus Osteotomy\n\n## INTRODUCTION\nAntibiotics are used to treat and prevent postoperative infections. In 1960, it was reported that pathogens are present during surgery[1],[2] regardless of how aseptic the surgery might appear. Moreover, the correlation between prophylactic antibiotics and postoperative wound infections was demonstrated. Therefore, prophylactic antibiotics are now used in almost all surgical procedures. The most effective method of antibiotic prophylaxis is the preoperative administration of antibiotics because it can act at the time when the wound is potentially contaminated by bacteria.[2]\u207b[4] On the other hand, it was also reported that the use of antibiotics after 3 - 4 hours of a bacterial invasion is unsuitable.[5]\n\nProphylactic antibiotics are generally administered both preoperatively and postoperatively. Hence, the effects of the indiscriminate method and period of administration are unclear, considering the multiple factors that contribute to postoperative wound infections.[6]\u207b[8]\n\nThe use of antibiotic prophylaxis is controversial even in orthognathic surgery, which is a representative procedure for oral and maxillofacial surgery. There are reports show no increase in the incidence of infection without the administration of postoperative prophylactic antibiotics.[9],[10] On the other hand, there are reports to suggest the necessity of continuous antibiotic administration.[11] However, orthognathic surgery is mainly performed on young patients without a specific medical history. Moreover, the number of factors associated with the development of postoperative wound infections decreases as the procedure becomes more generalized and its technique advances.\n\nThe aims of this clinical study were to evaluate the prevalence of postoperative wound infections with or without antibiotic prophylaxis after orthognathic surgery in young patients without any specific medical history, and to identify criteria for appropriate use of prophylactic antibiotics in orthognathic surgery.\n\n## PATIENTS AND METHODS\nFifty-six patients in their 20s without a specific medical history, and who were to undergo orthognathic surgical procedures at the department of oral and maxillofacial surgery at the dental hospital of Yonsei University were enrolled in this study. A horizontal maxillary osteotomy and vertical ramus mandibular osteotomy were performed by the same oral surgeon with the aid of trained nurses and residents under hypotensive general anesthesia. No bone grafts were performed. The duration of surgery was less than 5 hours. During surgery, maxillomandibular fixation was placed using steel wires, and drainage tubes were placed on both sides of the mandible. The drainage tubes were removed 2 days after surgery. The wires used for maxillomandibular fixation were removed and the sutures were taken out from the wounds 7 days after surgery. The patients received a non-steroid anti-inflammatory drug (Ketorolac trometamine 30 mg) intramuscularly immediately after surgery and every 6 hours until the next day. Compression bandages and ice packs were applied to the facial area until the second day after surgery.\n\nThe 56 patients were divided into 2 groups according to the randomization codes generated by Microsoft Excel: an experimental and control group. The patients in the experimental group received only 1.0 g of a third-generation cephalosporin (Cefpiramide) intravenously 30 minutes before surgery and did not receive the placebo. The control group also received 1.0 g of Cefpiramide 30 minutes before surgery as well as twice daily until 3 days after surgery. The patients were evaluated every day during the first 3 days and at the end of the 1st and 2nd week after surgery for any postoperative infections in reference to the criteria for defining a surgical site infection (SSI), recommended by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).[12] Postoperative wound infection was defined by at least 1 of the following criteria:\n\nStatistical analysis was performed using a \u03c7\u00b2-test on the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS for windows, ver. 12.0, SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA). The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the College of Dentistry, Yonsei University (YUDC).\n\n## RESULTS\nThe mean (SD) age of the experimental group was 23.9 years (5.84) with male-female ratio of 4 : 3. The average duration of surgery was 3 hours and 40 minutes. The mean (SD) age of the control group was 24.3 years (6.33) with male-female ratio of 1 : 1. The average duration of surgery was 3 hours and 55 minutes.\n\nThere were 3 infections in the experimental group and 2 infections in the control group, observed 2 weeks after surgery (Table 1). One patient in the experimental group was diagnosed with an infection by facial swelling, redness and sinus haziness in the waters' view, and the other 4 patients were diagnosed with a postoperative infection by swelling and redness, and pain on the mandibular area. Therefore, the wounds were opened by a surgeon and the patients were treated with antibiotics. However, only 1 patient in the control group developed wound dehiscence only without any drainage, fever, or swelling in the maxillary area. According to the \u03c7\u00b2-test, there was no significant difference in the prevalence of postoperative wound infections between the patients who had received postoperative prophylactic antibiotic administration and those who had not (p = 0.639).\n\n[Table 1: Results according to the Postoperative Antibiotic Prophylaxis \u2014 image only, no cells; see tables]\n\n## DISCUSSION\nThe method of antibiotic prophylaxis is determined by an evaluation of the patient, procedure, and surgical wound. The preoperative and immediate postoperative administration of antibiotics is a method generally used for antibiotic prophylaxis in almost all surgical procedures. However, antibiotics are continuously used postoperatively in most procedures because it is difficult to assess the factors associated with postoperative wound infections or appropriate antibiotic prophylaxis method.\n\nOn the other hand, orthognathic surgery is mainly performed on young patients without an underlying illness or comorbidity. Moreover, the number of factors affecting the development of postoperative wound infections decreases with the improvement of the surgical instruments, materials, techniques, and more generalized procedure.\n\nPeterson[13] suggested that the prophylactic antibiotic administration for postoperative wound infections in oral and maxillofacial surgery should be performed if there is a strong probability of infection, and appropriate antibiotics must be given in high-dose but for only a short period of time. Orthognathic surgeries are classified as clean contaminated procedures with postoperative wound infection of 10% to 15%, and Peterson[13] reported that an incidence of an anticipated infection in oral clean contaminated surgery could be reduced by using prophylactic antibiotics. Zijderveld et al.[14] suggested that the incidence of postoperative infections (52.6%) increased without the administration of prophylactic antibiotics. Martis and Karabouta[9] suggested that the routine use of prophylactic antibiotics in orthognathic surgery is unnecessary, and Lindeboom et al.[15] also suggested that the use of postoperative prophylactic antibiotics (clindamycin) is unnecessary in orthognathic surgery (SSRO). Furthermore, Fridrich et al.[16] and Baqain et al.[17] suggested that the long-term use of antibiotics does not decrease the frequency of postoperative infections. However, wide range of patient's age, small group size, and various osteomies may cause difficulties when precisely evaluating the efficacy of prophylactic antibiotics.\n\nTherefore, this study was undertaken to examine the prevalence of postoperative wound infections in young patients after orthognathic surgery (Le Fort I osteotomy and bilateral intraoral vertical ramus osteotomy) with or without the use of postoperative prophylactic antibiotics. Twenty eight patients were enrolled in each group. The samples were selected at a significance level of \u03b1= 0.05 and a test power \u03b2= 0.20. A smaller infection rate was set to 5%, and the difference in the estimated infection rate was set to 30%, based on previous report that the incidence of postoperative wound infection using prophylactic antibiotics, ranges from 5.6% to 33.4%.[17] In this study, wound infections were observed in both groups, however, the number was small. This was attributed to the followings: the patients were young without a specific medical history, patients had no preoperative wound infections, no bone graft had been performed during surgery, the surgical procedures such as IVRO were less traumatic with a short duration, the tissue trauma during surgery was minimal due to the systematization of orthognathic surgery and the improvement of techniques, and wound control such as postoperative blood or exudate was properly performed.\n\nThe types of antibiotics used are important factors to consider for prophylactic antibiotic treatment. Penicillin is the representative antibiotic used as a prophylaxis during intraoral surgery and for the primary treatment of dental infections. Spaey et al[18] suggested the use of amoxicillin-clavulanate along with drain usage during SSRO in a study of antibiotic administration. In this study, third-generation cephalosporin antibiotics were administered before surgery, which is believed to be a possible prophylactic antibiotic that may be used in orthognathic surgery because most bacteria cultured during a dental infection are susceptible to third-generation cephalosporin.[19] There has been an increase in infections due to anaerobic and Gram-negative organisms,[20] and most wound infections after orthognathic surgery are caused by Gram negative bacteria.[21]\n\nIf a post-operative wound infection occurs despite the effective prophylactic antibiotic administration before surgery, it could be concluded that the bacteria in the infected wound are not sensitive to the prophylactic antibiotics administered, and in such cases, an appropriate antimicrobial therapy should be determined by a culture test of the bacteria found in the infected region.[21],[22]\n\nProphylactic antibiotics reduce the risk of postoperative wound infections, which leads to a lower number of hospitalization days, reduced cost, and improved social life. However, the long-term use of postoperative prophylactic antibiotics may lead to several problems, such as various allergic reactions, increased cost, changes in resident bacterial colony in vivo, or appearance of resistant bacteria.[7],[23]\n\nMore studies with much larger numbers of patients are needed on the administration of prophylactic antibiotics during orthognathic surgery and other oral and maxillofacial procedures. In addition, further research on properly appropriated use of antibiotic prophylaxis is warranted in order to minimize the use of prophylactic antibiotics and their adverse effects and problems. In the present study, there was no significant difference in the prevalence of postoperative wound infections between patients who had received postoperative prophylactic antibiotic administration and those who did not. Therefore, prolonged prophylactic antibiotic use after orthognathic surgery may not be necessary, provided that there are no other significant factors for wound infections.",

input.text:
## RESULTS
The mean (SD) age of the experimental group was 23.9 years (5.84) with male-female ratio of 4 : 3. The average duration of surgery was 3 hours and 40 minutes. The mean (SD) age of the control group was 24.3 years (6.33) with male-female ratio of 1 : 1. The average duration of surgery was 3 hours and 55 minutes.

There were 3 infections in the experimental group and 2 infections in the control group, observed 2 weeks after surgery (Table 1). One patient in the experimental group was diagnosed with an infection by facial swelling, redness and sinus haziness in the waters' view, and the other 4 patients were diagnosed with a postoperative infection by swelling and redness, and pain on the mandibular area. Therefore, the wounds were opened by a surgeon and the patients were treated with antibiotics. However, only 1 patient in the control group developed wound dehiscence only without any drainage, fever, or swelling in the maxillary area. According to the chi2-test, there was no significant difference in the prevalence of postoperative wound infections between the patients who had received postoperative prophylactic antibiotic administration and those who had not (p = 0.639).

## DISCUSSION
Orthognathic surgeries are classified as clean contaminated procedures with postoperative wound infection of 10% to 15%. Zijderveld et al. suggested that the incidence of postoperative infections (52.6%) increased without the administration of prophylactic antibiotics. Twenty eight patients were enrolled in each group. The samples were selected at a significance level of alpha = 0.05 and a test power beta = 0.20. A smaller infection rate was set to 5%, and the difference in the estimated infection rate was set to 30%, based on previous report that the incidence of postoperative wound infection using prophylactic antibiotics, ranges from 5.6% to 33.4%.

input.paper_title: The Efficacy of Postoperative Prophylactic Antibiotics in Orthognathic Surgery: A Prospective Study in Le Fort I Osteotomy and Bilateral Intraoral Vertical Ramus Osteotomy

paper_metadata.authors: Sang-Hoon Kang, Jae-Ha Yoo, Choong-Kook Yi
paper_metadata.study_design: Prospective two-arm randomised controlled trial (allocation by Microsoft Excel randomisation codes); 56 patients, 28 per arm; primary outcome postoperative surgical site infection at 2 weeks, analysed by chi-squared test

studies.label: Postoperative prophylactic antibiotics vs none after Le Fort I osteotomy + bilateral IVRO

n_per_group.label: Control group, postoperative antibiotics for 3 days

sample_flow.reason: No exclusions, withdrawals or losses to follow-up are reported anywhere in the paper; there is no CONSORT flow diagram. The count is not stated, so no n is recorded here rather than recording 0.

variables.name: Age at surgery
variables.provenance_quote: Fifty-six patients in their 20s without a specific medical history, and who were to undergo orthognathic surgical procedures at the department of oral and maxillofacial surgery at the dental hospital of Yonsei University were enrolled in this study.

variables.name: Treatment arm (postoperative antibiotic prophylaxis)
levels: experimental group (preoperative dose only, no postoperative antibiotics)
control group (preoperative dose plus 1.0 g Cefpiramide twice daily until 3 days after surgery)
variables.provenance_quote: The 56 patients were divided into 2 groups according to the randomization codes generated by Microsoft Excel: an experimental and control group.

variables.name: Postoperative surgical site infection at 2 weeks (CDC criteria)
variables.provenance_quote: There were 3 infections in the experimental group and 2 infections in the control group, observed 2 weeks after surgery (Table 1).

variables.name: Wound dehiscence (recorded separately from infection)
variables.provenance_quote: However, only 1 patient in the control group developed wound dehiscence only without any drainage, fever, or swelling in the maxillary area.

variables.name: Duration of surgery
variables.provenance_quote: The duration of surgery was less than 5 hours.

hypotheses.statement: The prevalence of postoperative surgical site infection does not differ between patients receiving postoperative prophylactic antibiotics for 3 days and patients receiving only a single preoperative dose.
hypotheses.provenance_quote: The aims of this clinical study were to evaluate the prevalence of postoperative wound infections with or without antibiotic prophylaxis after orthognathic surgery in young patients without any specific medical history, and to identify criteria for appropriate use of prophylactic antibiotics in orthognathic surgery.

tests.location: Results, final paragraph; repeated in Abstract and Conclusion
tests.provenance_quote: According to the χ²-test, there was no significant difference in the prevalence of postoperative wound infections between the patients who had received postoperative prophylactic antibiotic administration and those who had not (p = 0.639).

findings.location: Table 1, Age (Mean±SD) row, experimental group column
findings.quote: Age (Mean±SD)  23.9±5.84 yrs  [experimental group without postoperative antibiotics (n=28)]
findings.notes: The bound is STATED by the paper, not assumed by me: the enrolment sentence restricts the sample to patients 'in their 20s', which is the interval [20, 29]. For n = 28 confined to that interval the largest attainable sample SD is 4.58; the reported 5.84 is 127% of that ceiling. The paper additionally leans on a narrow age range as a design strength, criticising prior work for 'wide range of patient's age', so the narrow-age claim is load-bearing in the authors' own argument rather than incidental. Note this row does not feed the primary chi-squared test, so it does not alter the headline p-value; it is a Table 1 data-integrity problem.

consequence.explanation: Undermines the reported baseline age description and the Discussion's claim that a narrow patient age range distinguishes this study from prior work; it does not touch the primary infection comparison.

findings.location: Table 1, Age (Mean±SD) row, control group column
findings.quote: Age (Mean±SD)  24.3±6.33 yrs  [control group with postoperative antibiotics for 3 days (n=28)]
findings.notes: Same stated bound as the experimental arm. Reported SD 6.33 is 138% of the 4.58 ceiling for n = 28 on [20, 29]. Both arms fail independently, so this is not a single mistyped cell.

consequence.explanation: Same as the experimental arm: the baseline age description and the narrow-age-range design claim cannot both hold, while the primary infection comparison is unaffected.

findings.location: Table 1, Age (Mean±SD) row, experimental group column
findings.notes: Rules out the most common innocent explanation. If 5.84 were a mislabelled standard error the implied SD would be 30.9 years, which is 6.7 times the ceiling and worse still. The tool returns likely_interpretation = 'neither', so no reading of the printed dispersion is compatible with an age range of 20-29.

consequence.explanation: Eliminates SD/SE confusion as an explanation for the impossible age dispersion, which narrows the remaining explanations to a wider-than-stated age range or a reporting error.

findings.location: Table 1, Age (Mean±SD) row, control group column
findings.notes: As with the experimental arm, neither the SD nor the SE reading clears the ceiling; under the SE reading the implied SD is 33.5 years.

consequence.explanation: Eliminates SD/SE confusion for the control arm as well.

findings.location: Table 1, Age row, control group column (sensitivity analysis)
findings.quote: Fifty-six patients in their 20s without a specific medical history
findings.notes: Robustness run against a deliberately over-generous reading of 'in their 20s' that admits an extra year at the top. The reported SD still exceeds the ceiling by 24%, so the finding does not depend on reading the inclusion criterion strictly.

consequence.explanation: Shows the impossibility survives a lenient interpretation of the stated age criterion.

findings.location: Table 1, Age row, control group column (bracketing analysis)
findings.notes: This is a bracketing run, not a check of a paper-stated value, hence indeterminate: it quantifies how far the data would have to depart from the stated criterion. A span of 12 years (20-32) still fails; 13 years (20-33) is the first that admits SD = 6.33, and even there the SD sits at 95.6% of the theoretical maximum, which is only attainable if patients are stacked almost entirely at the two extremes of the range. A realistic unimodal age distribution would need a wider span still. Either way the sample cannot be described as 'in their 20s'.

consequence.explanation: Quantifies the contradiction: reconciling the reported SD requires an age span of at least 13 years plus a near-bimodal distribution, contradicting the stated enrolment criterion.

findings.location: Results, final paragraph (also Abstract and Conclusion)
findings.quote: According to the χ²-test, there was no significant difference in the prevalence of postoperative wound infections between the patients who had received postoperative prophylactic antibiotic administration and those who had not (p = 0.639).
findings.notes: The paper's only inferential statistic reproduces exactly as an uncorrected Pearson chi-squared on a 2x2 table of 3/28 vs 2/28. This also resolves an ambiguity in the Results narrative: the p-value pins the tested counts to 3 vs 2, confirming the single wound-dehiscence patient was NOT counted as an infection event. The paper reports no chi-squared statistic and no df, only the bare p.

consequence.explanation: The reported p is arithmetically correct for the test the authors say they ran.

findings.location: Results, final paragraph; Methods, statistical analysis paragraph
findings.quote: Statistical analysis was performed using a χ²-test on the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS for windows, ver. 12.0, SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA).
findings.notes: Analysis-design mismatch (rulebook rule 5). Both infection cells have an expected count of 2.5, well below the conventional minimum of 5 for an uncorrected Pearson chi-squared, so the chosen test is not valid for this table; Fisher's exact test is the appropriate choice and returns p = 1.00 rather than 0.639. The paper reports no assumption check and does not mention Fisher's exact. This does NOT change the conclusion's direction: both tests are non-significant, so the substantive claim survives, but the reported p-value overstates the precision of the comparison.

consequence.explanation: The headline p = 0.639 comes from a test whose assumptions the data violate; the appropriate Fisher's exact p is 1.00, but the 'no significant difference' conclusion is unchanged.

findings.notes: Read with heavy caution. Tau-hat = 2.40 indicates under-dispersion, i.e. baseline arms more alike than randomisation typically produces (rulebook rule 1: high baseline p-values are the red flag, never reassurance), and the derived p-values are 0.81 and 0.59. But this Table 1 has only TWO baseline rows, which is far too few to estimate a dispersion multiplier reliably; the CSF cross-check returned indeterminate on the same p-values, and the tool caps below highly_suspicious without corroboration. Compounding this, the age row's p-value is derived from the very SDs shown to be impossible above, so one of the two inputs is known to be corrupt. Treat as weak corroborating context only, never as a standalone signal.

consequence.explanation: Suggestive of baseline over-similarity, but with only two rows and one corrupt input it cannot independently support any claim about the randomisation.

findings.location: Table 1 (all count rows) and Results, paragraphs 1-2
findings.quote: Sex (Male : Female) 16 : 12 / 14 : 14; Postoperative infection (n) 3 / 2; There were 3 infections in the experimental group and 2 infections in the control group ... One patient in the experimental group was diagnosed with an infection by facial swelling, redness and sinus haziness in the waters' view, and the other 4 patients were diagnosed with a postoperative infection
findings.notes: All 5 of 5 sums reconcile exactly with zero tolerance. The counts are internally coherent throughout: the sex ratios stated in prose (4:3 and 1:1) match the table's 16:12 and 14:14; both arms sum to 28 and to 56 overall; and the narrative breakdown of infected patients (1 with sinus haziness plus the other 4) sums to the 5 infections in Table 1. The count layer of this paper is clean.

consequence.explanation: No arithmetic discrepancy in any reported count; the event counts underlying the primary test are internally consistent.

findings.notes: Denominator is very small and the result carries correspondingly little weight: the paper contains exactly one table with exactly two (mean, SD) pairs, giving a single cross-block comparison. No duplication detected, but with one comparison this is close to uninformative and should not be cited as evidence of integrity.

consequence.explanation: No copy-paste signature, on a denominator of one comparison.

computed.error: GRIM does not apply to data_type='continuous'; it assumes integer observations on a bounded scale.

findings.notes: Recorded deliberately as a documented refusal rather than omitted. Age in years is a continuous ratio measure and the paper nowhere states that ages were recorded as whole years, so GRIM is not applicable and the tool correctly declines. I did NOT re-run it with data_type='integer' to force a verdict: had ages been whole numbers, 23.9 x 28 = 669.2 and 24.3 x 28 = 680.4 would both be non-integral and would fail GRIM, but that conclusion rests entirely on an assumption the paper never makes, and asserting it would be a false accusation. The age anomaly is established instead by the SD-range check, which rests only on the paper's own stated inclusion criterion.

consequence.explanation: No claim is affected; this records why a granularity check on age was not pursued.

findings.quote: According to the χ²-test, there was no significant difference ... (p = 0.639).

inputs.text: Results and Discussion body text extracted from the JATS XML

findings.notes: In this sweep statcheck was run with the `text` argument set to the Results/Discussion body text returned by extract_xml; the PDF-path command above is the equivalent runnable CLI form. Zero statistics were recovered, and this is a reporting finding rather than a tool failure: the paper never prints a test statistic or degrees of freedom anywhere, giving only a bare 'p = 0.639'. There is therefore no APA-form triple for statcheck to verify, and independent verification was only possible because the underlying cell counts appear in Table 1 (rulebook rule 10: cell counts outrank stated p-values).

consequence.explanation: No NHST result in the paper is stated in a form statcheck can audit; verification had to proceed from the raw counts instead.

findings.location: Discussion, paragraph beginning 'Therefore, this study was undertaken'
findings.quote: Twenty eight patients were enrolled in each group. The samples were selected at a significance level of α= 0.05 and a test power β= 0.20. A smaller infection rate was set to 5%, and the difference in the estimated infection rate was set to 30%, based on previous report that the incidence of postoperative wound infection using prophylactic antibiotics, ranges from 5.6% to 33.4%.
findings.reproduction: Not reproducible as a CLI command: verify_power_analysis requires an effect_size (Cohen's h for two proportions), which the paper does not state.
findings.reproduction_problem: verify_power_analysis takes `effect_size`; for test_type=two_proportions that is Cohen's h. The paper states raw proportions (5% and 35%) rather than h, and converting them requires an arcsine transform. Computing an effect size by hand is barred, so the check was not run rather than run on a self-supplied number.
findings.notes: Recorded as a refusal with its reason, not as a pass. Two observations that do not require any computation. First, the paper writes 'a test power β= 0.20': beta is the Type II error rate, so the power is 1 - beta = 0.80, and calling beta the power is a terminology error. Second, and more substantively, the stated design was sized to detect a difference between a 5% and a 35% infection rate, i.e. 30 percentage points. The observed contrast was 3 of 28 versus 2 of 28. A trial powered only for a 30-point difference cannot support a claim that no difference exists.

consequence.explanation: The sample-size justification behind the Conclusion's 'may not be necessary' claim cannot be reproduced from the printed inputs.

findings.quote: Conclusion: Prolonged prophylactic antibiotic use after orthognathic surgery may not be necessary, provided that there are no other significant factors for wound infections.

reported.confidence_interval: none reported anywhere in the paper

findings.reproduction: Not reproducible as a CLI command: absence-of-evidence requires ci_low and ci_high, and the paper reports no confidence interval for any quantity.
findings.reproduction_problem: absence_of_evidence requires a confidence interval. The paper reports no interval for the risk difference, the odds ratio, or any other effect measure, and deriving one by hand is barred. The check therefore could not run.
findings.notes: This is the paper's headline claim and it is an absence-of-evidence inference: a non-significant p from a 5-event trial is treated as evidence that postoperative antibiotics are unnecessary. The largest effect still compatible with these data cannot be bounded from anything the paper prints, because no interval is reported. The recalculation incidentally recovered a Fisher odds ratio of 1.56, i.e. the point estimate actually favours the arm that received postoperative antibiotics, but with 5 events in total the interval around it would be very wide. Severity is asserted, not computed: nothing here is arithmetically impossible, and the concern is inferential.

consequence.explanation: The Abstract's conclusion that prolonged prophylaxis 'may not be necessary' rests on a non-significant result from 5 total events with no interval to bound the effect it could be missing.

findings.quote: The patients in the experimental group received only 1.0 g of a third-generation cephalosporin (Cefpiramide) intravenously 30 minutes before surgery and did not receive the placebo. ... A horizontal maxillary osteotomy and vertical ramus mandibular osteotomy were performed by the same oral surgeon

reported.outcome_criteria: CDC SSI criteria including subjective signs: pain or tenderness, localized swelling, redness or heat, and 'Diagnosis of SSI by the surgeon or attending physician'

findings.reproduction: Not reproducible as a CLI command: this is a design observation read from the Methods, and no forensic tool evaluates blinding.
findings.reproduction_problem: No tool in the suite evaluates blinding or outcome-assessment bias; this is a methodological reading of the Methods section, recorded so it is not silently omitted.
findings.notes: Design context bearing on how much weight the 3-versus-2 event counts can carry. The trial was explicitly unblinded (no placebo), all operations were performed by one surgeon, and two of the four CDC criteria the authors adopted are subjective, one of them being diagnosis by the surgeon. Allocation itself was by Excel-generated codes, which is a reasonable randomisation method, so the concern is assessment rather than allocation. Severity is indeterminate because this is a qualitative judgement about bias risk, not a numeric anomaly, and it is asserted rather than computed.

consequence.explanation: Unblinded subjective assessment by the operating surgeon weakens the evidential value of the event counts but implies no specific direction of error.

findings.location: Patients and Methods, paragraph 1; Results throughout
findings.quote: Fifty-six patients in their 20s without a specific medical history ... were enrolled in this study.
findings.reproduction: Not reproducible as a CLI command: this records the absence of reported figures, and no tool checks for a missing CONSORT flow.
findings.reproduction_problem: The finding is the absence of numbers rather than a value to test; no forensic tool takes 'not reported' as an input.
findings.notes: Reporting gap recorded under rulebook rule 7. All 56 enrolled patients appear in the analysis with no exclusions, withdrawals or losses to follow-up mentioned, and there is no CONSORT flow diagram or trial registration number. Complete retention is not implausible over a 2-week postoperative window in a surgical cohort, so this is noted as a transparency gap rather than treated as a signal in itself. Note the group sizes 28/28/56 are not suspiciously round in the 50/100 sense, so no round-N concern arises.

consequence.explanation: Absence of flow reporting means the analysed sample cannot be independently reconciled against enrolment, though the reported counts are internally consistent.

unchecked.reason: The JATS XML reports Table 1 with image_only: true, n_rows: 0, width: 0 -- it is a picture in the XML and carries no cells at all. The grid was recovered from the PDF (page 3) as instructed and every value was checked, but the eight cell values are HAND-TRANSCRIBED from PDF text rather than machine-extracted: pdfplumber also returned no tables for this paper, rejecting all five page candidates as segmented prose. Transcription was verified against the prose in Results, which independently states the same means, SDs, sex ratios and infection counts. No table structure flag (alignment_uncertain) applied, since the XML table had no rows to flag.

verify_power_analysis was not run. It requires an effect_size, which for two proportions is Cohen's h; the paper states raw proportions (5%, 35%) and computing h requires an arcsine transform. Performing that arithmetic myself is barred, and supplying a self-computed effect size would make the tool's verdict unauditable. Recorded as a finding (power_analysis_not_reproducible) rather than silently skipped.

unchecked.location: Abstract Conclusion and Discussion, final paragraph
unchecked.reason: absence_of_evidence was not run. It requires ci_low and ci_high, and the paper reports no confidence interval for any effect measure -- not for the risk difference, not for an odds ratio. Deriving an interval by hand is barred. Recorded as a finding (negative_conclusion_without_interval).

multiplicity_report was not run, deliberately. The paper contains exactly one inferential test of one hypothesis; per the rulebook a single planned confirmatory test needs no correction, and running a multiplicity analysis on m = 1 would manufacture the appearance of a problem that does not exist.

grimu_check and grimu_coexistence were not run. The rank-sum granularity argument applies only to Mann-Whitney U / Wilcoxon p-values; this paper's only p-value comes from a chi-squared test, and applying GRIM-U to it would be the single most likely route to a false accusation.

The average duration of surgery is reported as '3 hours and 40 minutes' (experimental) and '3 hours and 55 minutes' (control) with no SD, no n-specific dispersion and no test. With no dispersion statistic and no comparison, no granularity or consistency check applies. The only stated bound, 'The duration of surgery was less than 5 hours', is satisfied by both values.

sprite_reconstruct was not run. SPRITE requires integer-valued observations, and the paper nowhere states that ages were recorded as whole years; forcing data_type='integer' to obtain a verdict would rest the result on an assumption the paper never makes. The same reasoning is recorded for GRIM in the grim_age_correctly_refused finding.

debit_check was not run on the sex rows. DEBIT requires a binary variable reported as a mean with an SD; sex here is printed as a male:female count ratio (16:12, 14:14), with no mean or SD, so the check has no applicable inputs. The counts were instead verified by check_summation_batch and enter the baseline dispersion analysis as a categorical row.
No supplementary files accompany this paper in the provided directory; only the XML and the PDF are present. Recorded as genuinely absent rather than present-but-unreadable.
